Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Redwood walked NeoHealth through Console tracing, request-inspector, and error-analysis workflows. Focus on how to correlate a failed patient-intake API call back to model invocation, view token-level latency, inspect KV cache hits/misses (transcribed sometimes as K-V cash), and play back requests to reproduce transient errors. Discussed security (SOC2, SSO, network egress), dedicated capacity vs hosted for p95 targets, and next steps for a trial org and benchmarking.

Topics covered:
- Console: request log drilldown, trace waterfall, correlation IDs
- Error analysis: function-call failures, truncated outputs, rate-limit/429 handling
- Debugging flows: request playback, request inspector, KV cache visibility, model variant fallbacks
- Ops: how to set alerts, export logs, link to Datadog / Splunk
- Security/Qs: SSO, KMS, private deployment options

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Sarah Kline (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have about 50 minutes, miguel is going to demo the console end-to-end—tracing, request inspector, and how you would debug a failed request. 
[00:12] Jenna Park (NeoHealth PM): Thanks, Sarah. We're particularly interested in seeing how we can tie a user-facing error to the model call—our support team needs a playbook.
[00:18] Miguel Ortega (Redwood SE): Totally. I'll share my screen. Quick note, if anything looks odd the auto-transcription sometimes says K-V cash instead of KV cache, and sometimes request IDs get cut off.
[00:27] Tom Wu (NeoHealth SRE): we get noisy spikes at 3am sometimes; we want to see tail latency and whether it's the model or our network.
[00:33] Miguel Ortega: Right, so first screen is Requests view — you'll see a list with timestamps, status codes, model name, and route. I'm going to filter to recent failed requests, you can use correlation id or session id. 
[00:45] Speaker 6: (muffled) how many users in the org demo?
[00:48] Miguel Ortega: This demo tenant has sample traffic. Ok selecting a 500-level error here — request ID 32d9f... you can expand.
[00:55] [00:55] Miguel Ortega: The expanded panel shows top-level info, but the Trace tab is where we get into the waterfall: you'll see sequence of steps—api gateway -> routing -> model call -> token-generation -> response assembly. Each step has timings. Notice the model-call span is marked in red, and p95 is high.
[01:10] Anita Rao (NeoHealth): Is that p95 for token generation or including queue time?
[01:14] Miguel Ortega: Good question — we break out queue wait vs execution. The console shows queue time, decode time, and kernel time; sometimes it transcribes kernel as kernel/kernal in the search. You can hover to see raw ms.
[01:24] [01:24] Miguel Ortega: In the metadata we also log the model variant and quantization profile used — helpful if we fall back to a lower-cost quantized variant during capacity constraints.
[01:33] Jenna Park: Can we see the prompt and the proto-response? Support wants to reproduce the exact input.
[01:38] Miguel Ortega: Yes, Request Inspector includes raw request payload (prompt + metadata) and the generated tokens (partial streaming). For PII you can toggle redact, and there's an audit link to see who viewed the payload. Note: in this tenant the redaction demo is simplified.
[01:50] Ravi Menon (NeoHealth Security): On that audit idea — where are logs stored and how long do they retain? We need to confirm retention and KMS key usage for encryption at rest.
[01:58] Miguel Ortega: Logs and traces are stored in the control plane by default; retention is configurable. For Private deployments you can choose customer-managed KMS and longer retention on-prem. I'll follow up with the security pack.
[02:09] [02:09] Miguel Ortega: Back to the request — click 'Trace' then 'Token timeline' and you can scrub across tokens to see when a stop token or error happened. Here there's an unexpected truncation at token 187.
[02:22] Tom Wu: Could that be a rate limit? We have bursts from background jobs.
[02:26] Miguel Ortega: The request metadata shows a 429 was attempted earlier on the same session for a different route — but this specific request shows an internal decode error from the runtime. We surface the internal error code and a stack-like snippet (it's not full kernel stack for security reasons). Sometimes the transcript spells it 'runt-ime' haha.
[02:40] [02:40] Miguel Ortega: There's a helpful 'Related requests' pane — shows other requests from same user/session within +/- 1 minute; you can bulk-download those for an incident.
[02:50] Jenna Park: Support would like an automated runbook — e.g., if internal decode error -> try playback -> if reproduces -> escalate to Redwood SE -> otherwise check KV cache misses.
[02:58] Miguel Ortega: Exactly — we have a runbook template and you can attach it to alert policies.
[03:05] [03:05] Miguel Ortega: Now I'll demo Playback — click 'Replay' and the console will re-run the same prompt against a pinned model version in a safe sandbox, returning the full response and debug headers. This helps confirm whether a transient condition (like GPU oom or quantization fallback) caused different outputs.
[03:19] Anita Rao: When you replay, does it charge customer tokens?
[03:22] Miguel Ortega: For hosted trials we don't bill replays in the demo, but in production replays count as requests — you can route them to a test model to avoid cost. Also important: we mask customer PII during playback by default unless SRE toggles it.
[03:33] [03:33] Tom Wu: About KV cache — can we see hit/miss ratio per key?
[03:36] Miguel Ortega: Yes, the Cache Insights tab shows hit rate over time, top keys, and per-request annotations marking whether a prefix was served from cache. That field sometimes shows 'kv cash hit' in the automated speech notes.
[03:46] [03:46] Miguel Ortega: Here you can also force-evict a key in the trial org for testing — useful if you suspect stale context.
[03:52] Jenna Park: We have a specific flow: patient intake -> insurance parsing -> eligibility call. If one model step fails the downstream UI shows a 502. Can we trace across services?
[03:59] Miguel Ortega: You can attach custom correlation IDs from your app when calling the API; the Console will link those to request traces so you can map to our model spans. We also have SDK helpers to auto-propagate trace ids.
[04:12] [04:12] Miguel Ortega: Now switching to Alerts — you can create a policy on model-call p95 > 1.2s or internal error rate > 0.5% and send to PagerDuty/Slack. Alerts include a link to a pre-populated incident bundle with the most likely failed requests.
[04:25] Ravi Menon: Do alert payloads expose token contents? That's a compliance no-no.
[04:29] Miguel Ortega: No, alerts include metadata and redacted snippets. Full payload access is gated by role-based access controls and audit logs.
[04:37] [04:37] Anita Rao: If we go to Dedicated, how different is the trace visibility?
[04:41] Miguel Ortega: Dedicated exposes the same console UX; logs can be forwarded to your SIEM (we have a Splunk/Datadog integration). You can also opt for private control plane where logs stay in your VPC.
[04:53] Jenna Park: competitor question — if we self-host, do we get the same tooling?
[04:58] Miguel Ortega: Self-hosting can give you control but you'll need to wire up tracing and playback yourself; Redwood's value is the integrated observability + runtime optimizations. (There was a brief mention of Anthropic and OpenAI during procurement chat earlier.)
[05:11] [05:11] Miguel Ortega: Ok, quick demo of a tricky case — intermittent 502 where request succeeded on replay. I'll open one: request id 7a9b2... See initial failure, then two subsequent successful plays. The trace shows a short kernel preemption event and a fallback to a lower-concurrency queue.
[05:25] Tom Wu: That helps. So if we see this in prod, do we get an automatic fallback?
[05:28] Miguel Ortega: Yes, policy-based fallbacks can route to a compatible model variant; you can set latency vs cost thresholds. We also have automatic canary rollbacks if a new model introduces regressions.
[05:38] [05:38] Jenna Park: On the replay result, can we export the exact prompt and tokens for legal review?
[05:42] Miguel Ortega: You can export as a jsonl bundle via the UI, but that export respects redaction policies and requires permission.
[05:48] [05:48] Speaker 6: (softly) do we get webhook for errors?
[05:50] Miguel Ortega: yes, webhook and event streaming available — we can push to your HTTP endpoint or to pub/sub.
[05:54] [05:54] Miguel Ortega: Last bit, the 'Request Timeline' view shows the entire org's span health over time — useful for incident retrospectives. You can annotate traces, add notes, and mark incidents closed.
[06:05] Jenna Park: This is exactly what support needs. 
[06:07] Sarah Kline: Great — quick recap: we'll send the runbook, Miguel will spin up trial org and demo playback with NeoHealth's sample dataset, and Ravi will share security checklist items. Any blockers on timelines?
[06:18] Ravi Menon: We need SOC2 artefacts and a network diagram.
[06:21] Miguel Ortega: I'll attach the security pack and a short gif of request inspector flow.
[06:25] Anita Rao: Also, can you show how the console links to our tracing system?
[06:29] Miguel Ortega: Yep — we have a small integration snippet for Datadog and Splunk that I'll include.
[06:34] [06:34] Sarah Kline: Ok, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the items in the action list.
[06:39] Jenna Park: Thanks, that was really helpful.
[06:41] [06:41] Miguel Ortega: One last note — if you want, we can run a short benchmark that measures p50/p95 for your real prompts against a few model variants; it usually takes an hour to set up.
[06:52] Sarah Kline: Perfect. We'll sync on dates. End of recording.
